title: GLP-1 Drugs Linked to Rare Eye Condition, but Absolute Risk Remains Very Low
excerpt: Two major studies confirm a small increased risk of sudden vision loss for Ozempic and Wegovy users, while regulators in Canada and Australia update safety labels.
body:
• Two new studies in the Annals of Internal Medicine found GLP-1 drugs are linked to a small increase in the risk of NAION, a rare eye condition that can cause sudden, permanent vision loss.
  • The absolute risk remains very low — roughly 3-4 extra cases per 10,000 patients over 18 months compared with other diabetes medications.
  • Health Canada and Australia have already updated safety guidance for GLP-1 medications to include NAION warnings, while the FDA continues to monitor the signal.
  • Researchers stress the findings should not change prescribing practices, as the cardiovascular and metabolic benefits of GLP-1 drugs far outweigh this rare risk.

Two large-scale studies published in the Annals of Internal Medicine have confirmed that GLP-1 receptor agonists — the blockbuster class of drugs that includes Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound — are associated with a small but real increase in the risk of a rare eye condition that can cause sudden vision loss.

What the Studies Found

Researchers from Rutgers University analyzed a large U.S. database of insurance claims from adults aged 18 to 65 with type 2 diabetes who started glucose-lowering medication. Compared with patients taking SGLT2 inhibitors or DPP-4 inhibitors, those treated with GLP-1 drugs had an increase of approximately three to four additional cases of ischemic optic neuropathy per 10,000 patients over an 18-month period.

"Although ischemic optic neuropathy was rare, it is clinically important because it can involve sudden vision loss," said lead author Chintan Dave, a faculty member at the Rutgers Institute for Health. "The increase in risk was small, but clinicians and patients should be aware of this potential association."

The condition — non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION — involves a sudden reduction of blood flow to the optic nerve, which can cause rapid and often permanent partial vision loss. Most cases in the study occurred in men or individuals between ages 50 and 65.

Swedish Data Corroborates Findings

A separate study from Sweden's Karolinska Institutet, analyzing nationwide healthcare data from more than 293,000 adults with type 2 diabetes, reached similar conclusions. After one year of follow-up, the risk of NAION was 0.04% among GLP-1 users compared with 0.02% among those taking SGLT2 inhibitors — a doubling in relative terms, but still extremely low in absolute numbers.

"Relative risk showed that there was double the chance of having NAION in the GLP-1 group compared to the SGLT2 group. That sounds very dramatic, but when you look at the absolute numbers, an increase of 0.02% is quite low."

— Dr. Benjamin Bert, Ophthalmologist, MemorialCare Orange Coast Medical Center

Regulators Respond

Health Canada and Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration have already strengthened safety guidance for certain GLP-1 medications to include NAION-related warnings. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration continues to monitor the evolving evidence but has not yet issued new labeling requirements.

A separate analysis using the World Health Organization's global drug safety database found that semaglutide users were 68.6 times more likely to develop NAION than those on other diabetes drugs — though researchers cautioned that reporting biases in pharmacovigilance databases can inflate such figures compared with controlled studies.

Should Patients Be Concerned?

Both study teams emphasized that the findings should not change current prescribing practices. "I would not recommend stopping a GLP-1 medication solely because of this study," Dave said. "These medications have substantial benefits for diabetes, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, and weight management, and the potential excess risk identified in our study was very small."

Patients who are older, male or have preexisting eye conditions may wish to discuss their individual risk profile with their clinician. The key warning signs of NAION include sudden, painless changes in vision — particularly dimming or blurring in one eye, loss of part of the visual field, or sudden vision loss — which should prompt urgent evaluation by an ophthalmologist.

What's Next

With GLP-1 prescriptions surging worldwide — Novo Nordisk's semaglutide alone generated $28.2 billion in revenue in 2025 — researchers say continued monitoring is essential. The observational nature of the current studies means a causal link has not been established, and confounding factors such as more advanced cardiovascular risk profiles among GLP-1 users may partly explain the association.
